lessons.title: Tour the rink
lessons.objective: Name the zones, lines, creases and circles so a broadcast makes sense.

payload.prompt: Tap the defensive zone (where your goalie is).

diagram.alt: A full hockey rink with the blue lines marking the zones and the red line at center.

explanation.correct: Right. Your defensive zone is where your goalie plays; the red center line divides it from the neutral zone.
explanation.incorrect: The defensive zone is the end with your goalie. The blue line marks where it ends and the neutral zone begins.

payload.prompt: Match each zone to what happens there.

pairs.definition: Where your goalie plays; the opposing team is attacking here.
Between the two blue lines; the transition area where play moves between zones.
Where the opponent's goalie plays; your team is attacking here.

explanation.summary: The three zones divide the rink into your end, the middle, and their end. This matters for offside and tactics.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're in their offensive zone pushing for a goal.

payload.prompt: Match the rink markings to their purpose.

pairs.definition: Marks the boundary between the neutral zone and the attacking or defensive zone; crucial for offside.
Divides the rink in half; also matters for some offside and icing calls.
The painted area directly in front of the goal; protects the goalie from interference.

explanation.summary: These lines define zones and protect the goalie, and they're key to understanding offsides and icing.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's in the crease, that would be goalie interference.

payload.prompt: How many players from one team can be on the ice at the same time during regular play?

options.text: Four
Five
Six

explanation.correct: Correct. Six skaters per team on the ice: usually three forwards, two defensemen, and one goalie.
explanation.incorrect: A hockey team has six skaters on the ice (not counting the goalie swap in some contexts): three forwards, two defense, one goalie. This makes it 6v6 during play.

payload.prompt: A hockey rink is 200 feet long and how wide?

options.text: 75 feet
80 feet
85 feet

explanation.correct: Exactly. An NHL rink is 200 feet long and 85 feet wide, creating a tight playing surface that rewards passing and positioning.
explanation.incorrect: The standard NHL rink is 200 feet by 85 feet. This narrow width means defense is compact and space is valuable.

lessons.title: Three periods and a stop clock
lessons.objective: Explain why a hockey game takes longer than 60 minutes.

payload.prompt: Guess: about how many minutes of stoppages happen in a typical period (penalties, injuries, goals, reviews)?

explanation.correct: Close. A period is nominally 20 minutes but with all the stops for whistles, penalties, injuries and celebrations, actual play is closer to 12–13 minutes.
explanation.incorrect: A 20-minute period has maybe 8–12 minutes of actual skating time once you subtract penalties, injuries, goals and other stoppages. This is why the game clock never stops.

payload.prompt: How long is a full hockey game from puck drop to final buzzer?

options.text: 60 minutes (3 x 20)
About 2 hours and 15 minutes with stoppages
Exactly 90 minutes

explanation.correct: Right. Three 20-minute periods plus two 15-minute intermissions (plus commercial breaks and stoppages) add up to roughly 2 hours 15 minutes in the real world.
explanation.incorrect: A game is three periods of 20 minutes each, plus two intermissions of 15 minutes each, plus stoppages. Total real time is about 2 hours 15 minutes.

payload.prompt: Complete the game structure.
payload.template: A hockey game has {{periods}} periods of {{minutes}} minutes each, separated by {{length}} intermissions.

explanation.correct: Right. Three 20-minute periods with 15-minute breaks. In overtime, the period is shorter (5 or 3 minutes depending on the league).
explanation.incorrect: Hockey is three periods of 20 minutes, with 15-minute intermissions between them.

payload.prompt: The clock stops when a player is injured. True or false?

scene.alt: A player is hurt during play, and the referee blows the whistle.

explanation.correct: False. The game clock never stops during play. An injury stops play (whistle), but the 20-minute clock keeps running.
explanation.incorrect: The clock runs the entire 20 minutes of each period, even when play is stopped for injuries, penalties or reviews.

payload.prompt: What happens during the intermission between periods?

options.text: Players rest, coaches draw up new plays, and the Zamboni resurfaces the ice
The teams switch ends and restart
Only the goalie comes off the ice

explanation.correct: Exactly. The 15-minute intermission lets players recover, coaches regroup, and the Zamboni cleans and resurfaces the ice so it's smooth for the next period.
explanation.incorrect: During the intermission, teams rest and rehydrate, coaches adjust strategy, and the Zamboni machine resurfaces the ice to keep it playable.

lessons.title: The faceoff, the tiny fight
lessons.objective: Describe how play starts and why centers matter on draws.

payload.prompt: How does play start at the beginning of a period or after a goal?

options.text: The goalie drops the puck
Two centers face off; the referee drops the puck between them
A winger throws the puck to center ice

explanation.correct: Right. A faceoff is when two centers (or other players if centers are in the box) line up and the referee drops the puck between their sticks.
explanation.incorrect: At the start of play or after a stoppage, the referee holds the puck at center ice and drops it between two opposing players (usually centers) who battle for possession.

payload.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The forward who plays in the middle of the ice, often the best passer, and takes most faceoffs for the team.
When a center gets their stick on the puck first at a faceoff and directs it to a teammate.
The moment when the referee drops the puck between two players to restart play.

explanation.summary: Faceoffs are where centers shine; winning the draw is about timing and stick position, and it often decides who gets the puck first after a stop.
explanation.sayThisLine: Our center won the draw and got it back to defense.

payload.prompt: Where on the ice do most faceoffs happen?

options.text: At the center red line only
In the faceoff circles near center, or in the zones when play stops there
Always directly in front of the net

explanation.correct: Right. There are five faceoff circles: one at center, two in each defensive zone. Play restarts in whichever circle is closest to where play stopped.
explanation.incorrect: Faceoffs happen at the center circle or in one of the four zone faceoff circles (two per end), depending on where the stoppage occurred.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: They're strong on the draw; we need our center to win it back and transition quick.

payload.question: What is she asking for?

options.text: To pull the goalie
To win the faceoff and quickly move the puck to attack or defend
To draw a penalty
To control play from the faceoff and start a breakout

payload.translation: The opponent's centers are good at faceoffs, so our center needs to win the puck first at the draw and then quickly pass to teammates to start an attack or exit the zone.

followUps.line: How good is your center on draws?
followUps.why: Tests if you know your team's strength.
Shows you know coaching prepares for them.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're new, ask what makes a center good at faceoffs.

payload.prompt: At the start of the game, the referee asks both teams if they're ready, then drops the puck. True or false?

scene.alt: The referee holds the puck above the ice between two centers who are ready to battle for it.

explanation.correct: True. Before each faceoff, the referee ensures both players are ready and in position, then drops the puck to start play.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the referee makes sure both centers are set and ready before dropping the puck. This prevents cheap shots and ensures a fair start.

lessons.title: Goals, shots, saves
lessons.objective: Tell a goal from a shot and a save, and read a box score line.

payload.prompt: Complete the scoring definitions.
payload.template: A {{goal}} is when the puck fully crosses the goal line. A {{shot}} is any attempt at goal. A {{save}} is when the goalie stops the shot.

explanation.correct: Right. A goal ends up in the net, a shot is any attempt, and a save is a goalie stopping it before it becomes a goal.
explanation.incorrect: A goal counts when the puck fully crosses the line. A shot is any attempt at goal. A save is the goalie making a stop.

payload.prompt: For a goal to count, what must happen?

options.text: The puck must touch the net
The puck must fully cross the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar
Any part of the puck must cross the line

explanation.correct: Exactly. The entire puck must fully cross the goal line between the goalposts and below the crossbar. If any part is still out, it's not a goal.
explanation.incorrect: The whole puck must completely cross the goal line between the posts and below the crossbar. The puck is in; the goalie is out. That's the rule.

payload.prompt: A shutout is when the goalie makes at least 30 saves. True or false?

scene.alt: A goalie has played well all game and the scoreboard shows zero goals allowed.

explanation.correct: False. A shutout is simply when your team's goalie allows zero goals in the game, regardless of save count. It's about the score, not the effort.
explanation.incorrect: A shutout means the opposing team did not score. The goalie could make 20 saves or 40; as long as the final score is 0 goals allowed, it's a shutout.

payload.prompt: If the final score is 4–2, what does that mean?

options.text: One team scored 4 goals and the other scored 2
One team had 4 shots and the other had 2
One team got 4 power plays and the other got 2

explanation.correct: Right. The score shows goals only: one team scored 4, the other scored 2. The game is over when time runs out or the difference is so large the trailing team gives up.
explanation.incorrect: The final score shows the goal total for each team. 4–2 means one team scored 4 goals and the other team scored 2.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We dominated; we had 35 shots and they had 8, but we only won 2–1.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team played better but scored less than expected
Her team's shots were much higher than the opponent's
Shot totals don't always match the final score
More shots always means winning

payload.translation: Her team controlled the game and took many more shots, but only converted 2 into goals while the opponent got lucky and scored 1. This shows the difference between shot volume and shot quality.

followUps.why: Asks if the opposing goalie was strong.

followUps.line: Were your shots from the slot or from the outside?
followUps.why: Shows you know shot quality matters.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It's natural to say 'we should have scored more'; this is a real hockey observation.

lessons.title: Assists and hat tricks
lessons.objective: Credit an assist correctly and know what a hat trick is.

payload.prompt: Complete the assist definition.
payload.template: An assist is awarded to up to {{count}} players on the scoring team who directly contributed to the goal.

explanation.correct: Right. Up to two players can be credited with an assist on a goal: typically the player who made the primary pass and the player who made the second-to-last pass.
explanation.incorrect: An assist goes to a player who passed to the goalscorer (primary assist) or to the player who passed to the passer (secondary assist). Usually two assists per goal, sometimes one.

payload.prompt: Player A passes to Player B, who passes to Player C, who scores. Who gets assists?

options.text: Player A only
Player B only
Players A and B

explanation.correct: Right. Player A gets the secondary assist (the pass before the final pass), and Player B gets the primary assist (the pass directly to the scorer).
explanation.incorrect: Player B gets the primary assist for the direct pass to the scorer. Player A gets the secondary assist for the pass before that.

payload.prompt: Match the accomplishments.

pairs.definition: When one player scores three goals in a single game.
A goal scored while the team has a player advantage due to an opponent's penalty.
A goal scored while the team is down a player due to a penalty.

explanation.summary: A hat trick is a special individual achievement; power-play and shorthanded goals happen in special situations.
explanation.sayThisLine: He just got his third goal—that's a hat trick!

payload.prompt: Why is scoring three goals called a 'hat trick'?

options.text: Players throw their hats on the ice to celebrate
It comes from a cricket tradition where a bowler who took three wickets was given a hat by sponsors
The player wears a special trick hat during the game

explanation.correct: Right. The term comes from cricket tradition and was adopted in hockey. When a player scores three goals, sometimes fans and teammates celebrate by tossing hats on the ice.
explanation.incorrect: A 'hat trick' originally came from cricket but now means any three achievements in one game. In hockey, when someone gets three goals, you might see hats tossed on the ice.

payload.prompt: One player can receive multiple assists in a single game. True or false?

scene.alt: A player celebrates after recording an assist and then later makes another pass that leads to a goal.

explanation.correct: True. A player can rack up assists all game long. Some high-end centers can have four or five assists in one game.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a single player can earn many assists in one game. It's one of the best ways for playmakers to contribute when they're not scoring.

lessons.title: Why players keep hopping the boards
lessons.objective: See why lines change constantly and how it can go wrong.

payload.prompt: Why do hockey players constantly come off the ice and get replaced by fresh players?

options.text: To rest their legs and manage their time on ice (shifts)
Because the rulebook requires it
To confuse the opponent

explanation.correct: Exactly. A shift for a skater is usually 30–60 seconds at full intensity. Players rotate off to catch their breath and hydrate; this keeps the team fast and fresh.
explanation.incorrect: Hockey is intense, and players tire quickly. Line changes keep everyone fresh so the team maintains speed and energy. A typical shift is less than a minute.

payload.prompt: Match the term to what happens.

pairs.definition: When fresh players hop over the boards to replace tired ones during play, without stopping the game.
A bench penalty when more than six skaters are on the ice at once; results in a power play for the opposing team.
The time one player or group spends on the ice before getting replaced by a fresh line.

explanation.summary: Line changes happen constantly to keep players fresh; 'too many men' is a penalty that can kill a team's momentum.
explanation.sayThisLine: They caught us changing, that's a too-many-men penalty.

payload.prompt: Line changes can only happen when play is stopped. True or false?

scene.alt: Players hop off the boards and fresh players jump on while the puck is still in play.

explanation.correct: False. Most line changes happen 'on the fly' during live play. Players sub themselves out and fresh legs jump in. This is a core tactical skill.
explanation.incorrect: Hockey is unique in that line changes happen constantly during play, not just at stoppages. This is called changing 'on the fly' and requires timing.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: They had a bad change down there and now they're defending on a long change.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The team's players are far from their bench, so they're tired
Fresh players couldn't get on the ice to relieve tired ones
The team is about to get scored on because of poor positioning
A line change took a penalty

payload.translation: When a line change doesn't work smoothly, the wrong players might be stuck defending far from their bench (a 'long change'). This is why bad changes are dangerous.

followUps.line: How did they recover from that?
followUps.why: Asks if the team survived the bad change.
Tests if you're tracking the consequence.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Bad changes are a real hockey risk; it's fine to ask what happened.

lessons.title: Whistles, puck over the glass, covered pucks
lessons.objective: Recognize the common reasons play stops.

payload.prompt: Order these events from most to least common during a game.

items.text: A shot misses the net and goes over the glass (puck out of play)
items.why: Happens frequently; out-of-play stops are common.

items.text: A penalty is called; the penalized player sits in the box
items.why: Penalties are regular but less frequent than out-of-play stops.

items.text: A goal is scored and play restarts with a faceoff
items.why: Goals are the rarest stoppages in most games.

items.text: A team shoots the puck down the ice from behind the red line (icing)
items.why: Icing is the least common; only happens when desperate or making a clearing play.

explanation.correct: Right order. Pucks going over the glass happen most often. Then penalties, goals, and icing.
explanation.incorrect: Pucks leaving the ice are the most common stoppage. Then penalties, goals, and icing follow in frequency.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pucks over the glass all night; that's why they say manage the puck.

payload.prompt: What happens when a player shoots the puck over the glass from anywhere?

options.text: It's a delay-of-game penalty
Play stops and the other team gets the puck
It's icing and no penalty

explanation.correct: Right. Shooting the puck over the glass from anywhere on the ice is a delay-of-game penalty and the player sits for two minutes.
explanation.incorrect: Shooting the puck out of play (over the glass) is a delay-of-game penalty. It's intentional stalling and the team loses the puck and a player.

payload.prompt: Match the stoppage type to the result.

pairs.definition: A player (usually the goalie) covers the puck with their glove or body; play stops and a faceoff is held.
A shot or pass leaves the playing surface; play stops and the other team gets possession in their zone.
A player is hurt during play; the referee stops the game so trainers can help.

explanation.summary: These stoppages reset play and protect player safety. Each has a specific restart method.
explanation.sayThisLine: The goalie smothered it; stoppage and a draw at the dot.

payload.prompt: When the goalie covers the puck with their glove, play stops immediately. True or false?

scene.alt: The goalie reaches out with their glove and catches the puck mid-play.

explanation.correct: True. The referee blows the whistle immediately when the goalie has control of the puck (glove save). This gives the team time to regroup.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, when the goalie has the puck covered with their glove or body, the referee stops play. This allows the team to catch their breath and set up for the faceoff.

payload.prompt: What is a common reason play stops in today's modern hockey (beyond injuries and penalties)?

options.text: Video review of a potential goal or penalty
Equipment malfunction (broken stick, helmet off)
All of the above

explanation.correct: Correct. Modern hockey stops for reviews (is it a goal?), for broken equipment (player safety), and for other safety reasons.
explanation.incorrect: Play can stop for video review, broken sticks, a helmet coming loose (player safety), or other issues that need to be fixed before play resumes.

lessons.title: Pulling the goalie
lessons.objective: Explain why a team removes its goalie late in a game.

payload.prompt: Pull the goalie or not? You're down by one with two minutes left.

situation.narrative: Your team is down 2–1 with two minutes left in the game. You have the puck in the neutral zone.

options.label: Pull the goalie and send a sixth attacker
options.consequence: You add an attacker, increasing offensive chances. The risk is an empty-net goal that makes it 3–1, but you're already losing.
considerations: You're down, so you have everything to gain by pulling.
An extra attacker increases the chance of scoring the tying goal.
An empty-net goal is bad, but you're losing anyway.

options.label: Keep the goalie in and play it safe
options.consequence: You stay 6-on-5 defensively. This makes scoring harder for your team and very likely means you lose.
considerations: Keeping the goalie in is too defensive when you're already behind.
You need scoring chances, not safety, with two minutes left.
Most coaches pull in this situation.

payload.expertNote: When you're down late in the game, pulling the goalie is almost always the right move. You're losing anyway, and the empty-net risk is worth the offensive upside.
payload.sayThisLine: Pull it and throw everyone forward. You need a goal.

payload.prompt: Why would a coach pull the goalie with two minutes left in a game?

options.text: To add an extra attacker and increase the chance of scoring
To rest the goalie
Because the goalie played poorly

explanation.correct: Right. Pulling the goalie swaps the goaltender for a sixth skater, creating a 6-on-5 advantage in forwards. This increases offensive chances but risks an empty-net goal.
explanation.incorrect: Pulling the goalie trades defense for offense. Instead of a goaltender, you put an extra attacker on the ice. You're gambling that you score before they do an empty-net goal.

payload.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Removing the goaltender from the ice and replacing them with a skater to add attacking power in a desperate situation.
A goal scored into an undefended net after the goalie has been pulled; a big risk of the strategy.
The additional forward or defenseman on ice when the goalie is pulled; increases offensive chances.

explanation.summary: Pulling the goalie is a high-risk, high-reward play used late in close games. One empty-net goal can end the game immediately.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're going to pull the goalie; we need to watch for an empty-net opportunity.

payload.prompt: An empty-net goal counts the same as any other goal. True or false?

scene.alt: An opponent skates down the ice and shoots the puck into the empty goal where the goalie usually stands.

explanation.correct: True. An empty-net goal is just a goal. It scores one point and can end the game in a close match. This is the gamble coaches take when they pull the goalie.
explanation.incorrect: An empty-net goal counts as a regular goal: one point on the score. The only difference is the opponent's puck goes into an undefended net.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: They should have pulled the goalie with three minutes left; instead they waited and got caught out.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The coach was too cautious and didn't add the extra attacker early enough
More time to score increases your chances of tying the game
The team missed an opportunity to get more shots
Goalies should always be pulled late in games

payload.translation: The coach hesitated too long before making the offensive gamble. Earlier in the final three minutes, pulling the goalie gives more time to generate scoring chances.

followUps.line: Did they score after the pull?
followUps.why: Tests if you're tracking the outcome.

followUps.line: How much time was left when they finally pulled it?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Timing the goalie pull is actually an interesting coaching debate; coaches genuinely disagree on when to do it.
